Subhuti, what do you think? If someone were to fill three thousand great thousand-fold worlds with the seven treasures <note>traditionally gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, red pearl, and cornelian</note> and give them all away in acts of <term>dana</term> <gloss>generous giving</gloss>, would this person gain much merit from such a cause? Very much, World-Honored One; this person would gain a great deal of merit from such a cause. Subhuti, if merit had a substantial reality, the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>Thus Come One; an epithet for the Buddha</gloss> would not say the merit is great. It is because merit is without substance <note>referring to the emptiness of inherent existence</note> that the <term>Tathagata</term> says the merit is great.

The merit derived from the seven treasures cannot bring about the realization of the <term>Buddha-fruit</term> <gloss>attainment of Buddhahood</gloss> or <term>Bodhi</term> <gloss>Enlightenment</gloss>, therefore it is said to be "nothing." Because it is immeasurable and limitless in quantity, it is called "much." If one could transcend it <note>reach the state of unconditioned merit</note>, then it would not be called "much."

### Section 20: Leaving Behind Form and Appearances
<note>This section discusses how the three bodies of the Buddha are complete, all marks are perfected, and both the self and the teachings are forgotten. This is not a physical completeness, hence it is titled Leaving Behind Form and Appearances.</note>

Subhuti, what do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by means of his perfected physical body? No, World-Honored One. As <unclear>page ends</unclear>

<summary>The text discusses the nature of merit, explaining that worldly offerings of treasure are empty of inherent substance, followed by a transition into the transcendence of physical forms.</summary>
